todayInHistory.title: Millions Spent Restoring Historic Day Peckinpaugh. Now it’s Barely Afloat
todayInHistory.text: The 259-foot Day Peckinpaugh, once envisioned as a floating museum, is in disrepair and could be sunk if its owner can't secure funding Day Peckinpaugh partially submerged. [Times Union] ERIE CANAL – The Day Peckinpaugh, built at Duluth and which once sailed the lower Great Lakes, rests partially submerged in the Hudson River just off the eastern shore on Friday, in Verplanck. The State Museum invested $4 million to restore the historic Erie Canal barge before auctioning it to a private buyer for $5,050 in late 2024. A legendary 259-foot-long motorship that once benefited from millions of dollars in state restoration funding is showing little more than its topside these days. Photographs obtained by the Times Union show the Day Peckinpaugh sitting just above the shallow waters of the Hudson River near a marina in the Westchester County hamlet of Verplanck. The images confirm the vessel’s current condition and location, which had drawn attention last week after a photograph was posted on the boat blog Tugster. Years after the State Museum invested $4 million to restore the ship, the state auctioned it off to private hands for just $5,050 in late 2024. The buyer, Capt. Dwayne Reith, confirmed that the photographs circulating online are authentic. Reith, head of Custom Marine in Dobbs Ferry, said the ship’s steel hull plates are in poor condition and its interior floods constantly. Day Peckinpaugh at Cleveland in 1995. todayInHistory.title: The McKee Sons’ Story is One of Ingenuity and Family Involvement
todayInHistory.text: Rob Alway writes about the laker McKee Sons and the key role the McKee family has played in Great Lakes shipping in his Great Lakes Boat Blog. McKee Sons in 1974. [Roger LeLievre] MUSKEGON, MI – On a recent visit to Muskegon, Michigan, I had the opportunity to tour one of the most interesting vessels remaining on the Great Lakes, a ship that began her life serving the United States during World War II, was transformed into a Great Lakes bulk carrier, and later became a self-unloading barge. The McKee Sons has been docked at Muskegon’s historic Mart Dock for nearly 12 years. Although she has not carried cargo since 2012, the vessel remains a remarkable example of American shipbuilding and the ingenuity of the Great Lakes maritime industry. The ship also represents nearly a century of the McKee family’s involvement in Great Lakes shipping and the ingenuity of its members. My guide for the visit was Patrick McKee, vice president of Sand Products Corp., the family-owned Muskegon company that owns the vessel through its Lake Service Shipping division. Lake Service Shipping’s only vessel is the McKee Sons. PART ONE: From troop transport to lake freighter: The remarkable journey of the McKee Sons. Read the story here PART TWO: Freighter to barge: The McKee Sons’ second life: Read the story here . PART THREE: A century of McKee family maritime history on the Great Lakes: Read the story here .

marineWeather.synopsis: 30.6 inch ridging continues over Lake Superior through Thursday morning as a 30.7 inch high pressure center moves east over New England and the Canadian Maritimes. A 29.4 inch Atlantic Low moves onshore over the Carolinas during this time, bringing 30.2 inch troughing over Lake Superior by Thursday afternoon. A gradient of 29.7-29.9 inch troughing (highest west) sets up over Superior by Friday morning as the Atlantic Low moves over the eastern Great Lakes, weak ridging builds over the Plains, and a 29.5 inch low develops over Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Troughing over the Great Lakes deepens as the Manitoba low moves eastward into Ontario and deepens to 29.4 inches by Saturday morning. Pressure begins to rise again Saturday afternoon as the Manitoba low moves out of the area and ridging builds over the Rockies. Ridging of 30.0-30.1 inches is expected to return over the Great Lakes Monday evening.

Strong high pressure around 30.8 inches will remain well to the east of the region today into tonight, while low pressure around 29.7 inches moves northward from Florida into North Carolina and strengthens to around 29.3 inches. Low pressure will continue to shift northward into the eastern Great Lakes region by Friday. East northeast winds will continue into tonight, becoming northeast and gusty over the southern half of the lake Thursday. Brisk north winds should occur Thursday night into early Friday, becoming northwest Friday afternoon, as the low passes by to the southeast and east. Gale force gusts are likely across the southern quarter of open waters from later Thursday afternoon into Friday morning. Gusty winds will continue through the weekend out of the southwest Saturday and northwest Sunday.
